The United Airlines aviation growth surge 2026 represents a pivotal moment in global travel, as the carrier spearheads a massive expansion across US, European, and Asian airports. By strategically increasing its flight frequencies and debuting new long-haul routes, United is positioning itself as the primary bridge between major financial hubs and emerging markets. This 2026 aviation growth is fueled by a robust recovery in business travel and a historic rise in leisure demand, forcing an accelerated modernization of terminal infrastructure and digital check-in systems.

For travelers and stakeholders, this expansion signifies more than just more flights; it marks a shift toward global connectivity and operational efficiency. United’s integration with Caribbean and Latin American airports specifically targets high-growth tourism corridors, ensuring that the airline captures a larger share of the transatlantic and transpacific markets. As the leading US airline in international capacity, United’s 2026 roadmap sets the pace for the industry, emphasizing sustainable aviation fuels and next-generation fleet deployment to maintain its competitive edge in a rapidly evolving airspace.

United Airlines Aviation Growth Surge 2026: A Global Overview

The massive scale of the United Airlines aviation growth surge 2026 is transforming how passengers traverse continents. By adding dozens of daily departures from leading US airports like Newark and Chicago O’Hare, the airline is effectively shortening the distance between the Western Hemisphere and European aviation hubs. This growth is supported by a significant fleet expansion, including the delivery of advanced, fuel-efficient aircraft designed for ultra-long-haul journeys.

Network Density: Increased frequency on established routes ensures that United Airlines 2026 remains the top choice for corporate travelers requiring flexible schedules.

Economic Impact: The expansion is projected to generate thousands of jobs across US and Asian airports, stimulating local economies through increased tourism and cargo logistics.

Strategic Expansion Across US and European Aviation Hubs

The cornerstone of the 2026 aviation growth is the strengthening of the transatlantic corridor. United has secured additional slots at European airports in London, Paris, and Frankfurt, allowing for a seamless transition for passengers connecting from the United States. This strategic move counters rising competition from low-cost carriers by offering premium services and extensive loyalty program benefits that only a global leader can provide.

Terminal Optimization: Investments in European airport infrastructure allow United to offer exclusive lounge access and expedited security for its Polaris passengers.

Code-Share Synergy: Enhanced partnerships with European carriers ensure that United Airlines provides the most comprehensive reach into secondary European cities.

Connecting the East: United’s Dominance in Asian Airports

As travel demand in the East reaches record highs, United is significantly broadening its footprint in Asian airports such as Tokyo-Narita, Seoul-Incheon, and Singapore-Changi. The 2026 aviation surge includes new non-stop flights that bypass traditional stopovers, saving travelers hours of transit time. This pivot toward Asia reflects a long-term commitment to the world’s fastest-growing economic region.

Market Penetration: United is tapping into the “VFR” (Visiting Friends and Relatives) market, which remains a resilient segment of Asian aviation growth.

Technological Integration: Implementation of biometric boarding in Asian airports has reduced boarding times by nearly 20%, enhancing the overall passenger experience.

The Caribbean and Latin American Aviation Growth Corridor

Focusing on the southern hemisphere, United is capitalizing on the Caribbean and Latin American aviation boom. By partnering with local authorities to upgrade Caribbean airports, the airline is facilitating easier access to top-tier vacation destinations. Simultaneously, its expansion into Latin American airports supports the region’s growing status as a hub for near-shoring and international trade.

Seasonal Adaptability: United’s ability to pivot capacity toward the Caribbean during winter months maximizes aircraft utilization and profitability.

Regional Connectivity: New routes to secondary Latin American cities provide vital links for business sectors ranging from agriculture to technology.

Future-Proofing Aviation: Sustainable Growth and Innovation

The United Airlines 2026 growth isn’t just about volume; it’s about the quality of the journey and the sustainability of the industry. The airline is leading the charge in adopting Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) across its global network. This commitment ensures that the aviation growth surge does not come at the expense of environmental goals, appealing to the modern, eco-conscious traveler.

Green Fleet: The retirement of older, less efficient planes in favor of the latest Boeing and Airbus models significantly lowers the carbon footprint per passenger.

Digital Transformation: Enhanced AI-driven scheduling tools help United Airlines minimize delays and optimize fuel consumption across all international airports.

United Airlines 2026 Global Expansion Key Details

Key Strategic Interpretations

Market Dominance through Niche Routing: United is intentionally targeting “secondary” European markets (like Bari and Split) where it can maintain a monopoly on nonstop US service, forcing competitors to rely on connecting flights.

Infrastructure Synergy: The surge in flights to Asian and European airports is timed with terminal upgrades and the rollout of the A321XLR, which allows United to fly long distances with narrow-body efficiency.

Regional Rivalry: The aggressive addition of routes at Chicago O’Hare specifically targets market share from American Airlines, using high frequency to win over corporate travelers.

Sustainability as a Branding Tool: By prioritizing the A321XLR and 787 Dreamliner, United is positioning its 2026 growth as “responsible expansion,” appealing to ESG-focused investors and eco-conscious passengers.

Conclusion

The 2026 aviation landscape is being redefined by United Airlines’ aggressive and strategic global expansion. By prioritizing network density in the US and Europe, while simultaneously capturing the high-growth potential of Asian and Latin American markets, United is setting a new standard for international air travel. This surge not only benefits the airline but also acts as a catalyst for infrastructure improvements and economic development across every continent it serves.

text:
Hanoi is preparing to introduce phased restrictions on fossil fuel-powered vehicles within the capital’s central wards as part of a low-emission zone (LEZ) initiative aimed at reducing air pollution and accelerating the transition to green transport.

Under a draft resolution submitted to the Hanoi People’s Council, which is expected to be reviewed at a special session opening on May 12, the city will gradually limit the use of gasoline-powered vehicles in areas inside Ring Road 1.

For private gasoline-powered motorcycles, excluding ride-hailing motorbikes, residents in pilot areas will be required to register online with local authorities regarding their vehicle transition plans between July 1 and October 1, 2026.

The first phase, running from July 1 to December 31, 2026, will cover the core area of Hoan Kiem Ward, including 11 major streets such as Trang Tien, Hang Khay and Le Thai To. During the pilot period, gasoline motorcycles will be restricted from operating between 6 pm and midnight on Fridays, and from 6 am to midnight on weekends. Gasoline-powered ride-hailing motorbikes are expected to be completely banned from the low-emission zone starting July 1, 2026.

The second phase, from 2027, will expand the pilot zone to include Hoan Kiem and Cua Nam wards. By 2028–2029, the entire area inside Ring Road 1—spanning nine wards —is expected to be designated a low-emission zone.

The proposal also includes stricter emissions regulations for freight vehicles. Trucks under two tons that fail to meet Level 4 emissions standards would be prohibited from entering the zone, while compliant vehicles would face peak-hour restrictions. Larger trucks would face tighter operating-hour limits or full bans.

According to Hanoi authorities, gasoline-powered motorcycles currently account for 94–97% of vehicles in the affected wards, underscoring the scale of the transition challenge. Officials have called for stronger financial incentives, tax reductions and registration fee exemptions for green vehicles, alongside expanded charging infrastructure and clearer transition policies to build public support.

To support implementation, Hanoi plans to accelerate the development of electric buses, urban railways, public bicycles and shared electric motorbikes, while installing charging stations and automated license plate recognition systems to monitor vehicle access and enforce regulations.

title: Kolaborasi TRKI UNDIP Bersama PT KPI Menuju Industri Hijau Berkelas Dunia
description:
Rombongan Program Studi Teknologi Rekayasa Kimia Industri (TRKI) Sekolah Vokasi Universitas Diponegoro hadir dengan energi besar dan semangat kolaborasi luar biasa.
Fahmi Arifan, S.T., M.Eng., IPM., MM., ASEAN Eng., Dr. Heny Kusumayanti, S.T., M.T., Yusuf Ma'rifat Fajar Azis, S.T., M.T., Sri Risdhiyanti Nuswantari, S.Tr.T., M.T., Dr. (cand) Abdullah Malik Islam Filardli, S.T., M.T., Dr. (cand) Teguh Riyanto, S.T., M.T., Sri Pudjawati, S.H., Nurul Pudiastutiningtyas, S.T., Nanik Kartikasari, S.T., Wahyu Widyati, A.Md., dan Aris Darmanto.
Rombongan TRKI disambut hangat oleh jajaran manajemen KPI seperti Bapak Budi Hermawan selaku HRD & GA Director, Bapak Pradhika Rama Ulianto selaku Production & Technical Director, serta Bapak Kus Heryadi selaku General Manager Technic.
Harus ada dampak nyata, inovasi nyata, dan transformasi nyata.
Kunjungan ini membuktikan bahwa TRKI Vokasi UNDIP tidak hanya hadir sebagai program studi, tetapi telah berkembang menjadi pusat inovasi vokasi yang aktif membangun sinergi strategis bersama industri nasional.
text:
Begitu roda pesawat menyentuh landasan Bandara Sultan Aji Muhammad Sulaiman Balikpapan pada Selasa, 5 Mei 2026, suasana langsung terasa berbeda. Ini bukan sekadar kunjungan industri biasa. Ini seperti "roadshow Avengers versi teknik kimia vokasi" --- bedanya bukan menyelamatkan bumi dengan palu Thor, tetapi dengan inovasi, riset terapan, efisiensi energi, dan ide-ide industrial sustainability yang bikin ruang meeting mendadak terasa seperti forum masa depan dunia energi Indonesia.

Rombongan Program Studi Teknologi Rekayasa Kimia Industri (TRKI) Sekolah Vokasi Universitas Diponegoro hadir dengan energi besar dan semangat kolaborasi luar biasa. Dipimpin langsung oleh Kaprodi TRKI, Dr. Mohamad Endy Julianto, S.T., M.T., bersama Hermawan Dwi Ariyanto, S.T., M.Sc., Ph.D. selaku Sekretaris Program Studi, rombongan dosen dan tenaga kependidikan terbaik TRKI bergerak dari Semarang menuju Balikpapan, Bontang, hingga kawasan IKN membawa satu misi penting: menjadikan pendidikan vokasi sebagai pusat lahirnya solusi nyata industri masa depan.

Turut hadir dalam rombongan tersebut Dr. Ir. Fahmi Arifan, S.T., M.Eng., IPM., MM., ASEAN Eng., Dr. Heny Kusumayanti, S.T., M.T., Yusuf Ma'rifat Fajar Azis, S.T., M.T., Sri Risdhiyanti Nuswantari, S.Tr.T., M.T., Dr. (cand) Abdullah Malik Islam Filardli, S.T., M.T., Dr. (cand) Teguh Riyanto, S.T., M.T., Sri Pudjawati, S.H., Nurul Pudiastutiningtyas, S.T., Nanik Kartikasari, S.T., Wahyu Widyati, A.Md., dan Aris Darmanto. Kombinasi ini benar-benar seperti "dream team" vokasi UNDIP --- lengkap, solid, dan penuh semangat membangun jejaring industri nasional.

Kunjungan ke PT Kaltim Parna Industri (KPI) menjadi salah satu momen paling strategis dalam perjalanan tersebut. Perusahaan amonia raksasa yang berlokasi di Kawasan Industri Kaltim, Bontang, ini dikenal sebagai salah satu industri petrokimia nasional dengan kapasitas produksi sekitar 530.000 ton amonia per tahun dan teknologi kelas dunia berbasis Haldor Topsoe serta Mitsubishi Heavy Industries. Bahkan KPI menjadi perusahaan pertama di Indonesia yang menerapkan Closed Sea Cooling Tower sebagai bagian dari komitmen lingkungan berkelanjutan. Keren? Jelas. Tapi yang lebih keren lagi adalah ketika dunia industri bertemu dunia vokasi dalam satu frekuensi visi besar.

Rombongan TRKI disambut hangat oleh jajaran manajemen KPI seperti Bapak Budi Hermawan selaku HRD & GA Director, Bapak Pradhika Rama Ulianto selaku Production & Technical Director, serta Bapak Kus Heryadi selaku General Manager Technic. Diskusi yang terbangun terasa sangat hidup, penuh gagasan strategis, dan jauh dari suasana formal yang kaku. Yang dibahas bukan hanya soal kunjungan mahasiswa atau magang biasa, tetapi bagaimana membangun ekosistem kolaborasi jangka panjang antara kampus vokasi dan industri energi nasional.

Dalam kesempatan tersebut, Dr. Mohamad Endy Julianto menyampaikan bahwa perguruan tinggi vokasi saat ini tidak lagi hanya menjadi "pabrik lulusan", tetapi telah bergerak menjadi co-creator solusi industri. Melalui pendekatan Project-Based Learning berbasis problem solving, mahasiswa TRKI dilatih langsung menyelesaikan persoalan nyata industri mulai dari optimasi proses, efisiensi utilitas, keselamatan berbasis HSE, hingga pendekatan green industry dan circular economy.

Bahkan salah satu topik yang paling menarik perhatian adalah gagasan pemanfaatan 85% sisa buangan CO KPI menjadi peluang ekonomi baru berbasis integrated low-carbon chemical industry. Ide pengembangan green methanol, dry ice, food grade CO, microalgae, hingga sustainable aviation fuel menjadi pembahasan yang sangat visioner. Bayangkan... gas buangan yang biasanya dianggap "musuh lingkungan" justru bisa berubah jadi peluang bisnis masa depan. Ini benar-benar definisi "jangan remehkan mantan... eh maksudnya jangan remehkan CO."

Diskusi menjadi semakin menarik ketika dibahas peluang integrasi CSR industri dengan teaching factory, laboratorium terapan, sertifikasi mahasiswa, hingga riset-riset aplikatif berbasis kebutuhan industri. Semua sepakat bahwa kolaborasi kampus dan industri tidak boleh berhenti di seremoni foto bersama dan tukar plakat saja. Harus ada dampak nyata, inovasi nyata, dan transformasi nyata.

Kunjungan ini membuktikan bahwa TRKI Vokasi UNDIP tidak hanya hadir sebagai program studi, tetapi telah berkembang menjadi pusat inovasi vokasi yang aktif membangun sinergi strategis bersama industri nasional. Dari Semarang menuju Balikpapan dan Bontang, langkah ini bukan sekadar perjalanan akademik, melainkan bagian dari perjalanan besar membangun masa depan industri Indonesia yang lebih hijau, modern, adaptif, dan berdaya saing global.

Dan mungkin di situlah bagian paling "wooo" dari semuanya --- ketika dosen, tendik, industri, mahasiswa, teknologi, hingga ide-ide masa depan bertemu dalam satu meja diskusi, Indonesia sebenarnya sedang menulis bab baru tentang kebangkitan vokasi dan industri nasional.

text:
In the face of rising fuel prices, South African motorists can now enhance their car-buying strategy with new tools that reveal just how much fuel efficiency can save them annually—potentially over R7,000. Will consumers adapt their choices to secure a more economical driving future?

Image: Supplied

As fuel prices continue their relentless ascent, South Africans are finding themselves at a crossroads regarding vehicle ownership.

The latest fuel hike has prompted consumers to shift their focus from the initial purchase price of vehicles to the ever-increasing costs associated with fuel consumption and overall ownership.

This shift is underscored by a growing awareness of fuel efficiency as a critical factor in car-buying decisions.

Antoine Caradonna, managing director of VehicleSA, noted the palpable shift in consumer mindset.

"While electric vehicles are capturing interest, they remain financially out of reach for many. Buyers are now asking a more practical question: can I afford to drive this car every day?"

With everyday expenses weighing heavily on household budgets, the need for economical driving has never been more pronounced.

In response to this growing concern, VehicleSA has launched an innovative monthly fuel cost calculator, intended to assist consumers in making informed decisions.

Unlike traditional comparison tools that solely rely on theoretical fuel consumption figures, this new calculator takes into account real-time fuel prices and individual driving habits.

Consumers can plug in their desired mileage, revealing personalised estimates that allow them to consider fuel expenditure alongside other essential ownership costs, such as repayments and insurance.

This holistic approach reinforces the importance of understanding the true cost of vehicle ownership.

VehicleSA has also unveiled a comprehensive ranking system highlighting the "cheapest cars to run" across key vehicle segments, all based on an average monthly driving distance of 1,250 km at current fuel prices.

The data compellingly demonstrates variations in fuel costs even among similar models.

For instance, in the hatchback category, fuel expenses for the popular Toyota Vitz and Suzuki Celerio amount to approximately R1,398 monthly.

In striking contrast, the less efficient Renault Kwid can escalate to R1,631 monthly, a difference that can accumulate to more than R7,000 in savings annually for those who opt for the more fuel-efficient options.

A similar pattern emerges in the crossover segment.

The Renault Kiger stands out as one of the most affordable options to run, averaging around R1,664 monthly in fuel costs.

Conversely, larger or less efficient models can inflate fuel bills by over R300 per month.

Caradonna added, “Even within the same brand, moving up a model range can significantly increase your fuel spend.”

The launch of VehicleSA's tools may provide the crucial guidance needed to navigate this challenging landscape, highlighting that when it comes to car ownership, understanding fuel efficiency could lead to significant savings over time.

title: Global Jet Fuel Crisis 2026: How Rising Aviation Costs are Threatening African Economies

text:
In the spring of 2026, the global aviation industry is finding itself in the eye of a geopolitical storm. What began as localized tension in the Middle East has rippled across the planet, manifesting as a severe jet fuel crisis that is doing more than just delaying vacations. It is reshaping the way the world moves and, more critically, placing a stranglehold on the burgeoning economies of Africa.

As shipping routes through the strategic Strait of Hormuz face unprecedented threats, the “lifeblood” of international travel—Jet A1 fuel—has become a scarce and expensive commodity. For the average traveler, this means higher ticket prices; for African nations, it represents a looming economic catastrophe.

A World Interconnected by Risk

The current crisis underscores a terrifying reality: the world’s air travel infrastructure is incredibly vulnerable to supply shocks. Market analysts report that global shipments of jet fuel have plummeted to record lows. The reason is largely geographic. Nearly 41% of Europe’s aviation fuel is linked to oil that must pass through the Strait of Hormuz. When that artery is restricted, the heart of global travel skips a beat.

The immediate fallout has been a doubling of aviation fuel costs in just a few short months. This isn’t just a balance sheet issue for airlines; it’s a survival crisis. Major global carriers like Lufthansa have already been forced to axe thousands of flights. Icons of the sky, including British Airways and Virgin Atlantic, have had no choice but to pass these skyrocketing operational costs onto passengers through steep fare increases.

The New Face of Global Travel

For the everyday traveler, the “golden age” of cheap long-haul flights seems to be retreating into the distance. We are witnessing a fundamental shift in how people plan their journeys:

The Death of the “Spontaneous” Trip: With fares surging, travelers are abandoning last-minute getaways and long-haul intercontinental dreams.

Regionalism Over Globalism: There is a marked pivot toward short-haul and regional travel. People are staying closer to home, choosing destinations they can reach without crossing three time zones.

Hub-Centric Flying: Travelers are being forced to route through major international hubs, as airlines cut “secondary” or smaller routes to save on fuel, leaving smaller cities increasingly isolated.

Africa: The Epicenter of the Economic Shock

While a European or American traveler might grumble about an extra £200 on a ticket, for many African nations, the crisis is far more existential. Many African economies are heavily dependent on imported petroleum products. Unlike wealthier nations that can dip into strategic reserves or rely on domestic refining, much of Africa remains exposed to the raw volatility of the global market.

In Africa, the cost of jet fuel doesn’t just affect the wealthy flying to business meetings; it acts as an inflationary multiplier. When fuel prices rise, the cost of transporting food, essential medicines, and fertilizers rises with it. This deepens the financial strain on already fragile economies, pushing millions closer to the poverty line.

The Nigerian Perspective: A Domestic Struggle

Nigeria serves as a poignant case study for this crisis. The nation’s domestic aviation sector, already battling foreign exchange volatility and infrastructure deficits, is now at a breaking point.

Domestic carriers in Nigeria have issued stark warnings: the rising cost of Jet A1 fuel is no longer just a “challenge”—it is a threat to their continued existence. Local ticket prices have surged to levels that make air travel a luxury many average Nigerians can no longer afford. This isn’t just about holidays; it’s about the suspension of business travel that drives the economy, the disruption of family reunions, and the stalling of religious pilgrimages.

When the planes stop flying in a country as large as Nigeria, the gears of commerce begin to grind to a halt.

Is There a Silver Lining?

Experts agree that the world is unlikely to “run out” of fuel entirely. Supply chains are resilient, and alternative routes are being explored. However, the current crisis serves as a loud wake-up call for the industry to accelerate its transition away from a total reliance on traditional fossil fuels.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and regional refining capabilities are no longer just “green” goals; they are now matters of national security and economic stability.

The Human Element

Beyond the data and the geopolitical maps, there is a human story. It’s the story of the small business owner in Lagos who can no longer afford to fly to meet suppliers. It’s the story of the family in London who has had to cancel a long-awaited reunion in Nairobi.

As we navigate the turbulence of 2026, the jet fuel crisis reminds us that in a globalized world, a conflict in one corner of the map can quiet the skies in another. The challenge for the coming years will be building a travel industry that isn’t just fast and far-reaching, but resilient enough to withstand the winds of political change.

title: Global Jet Fuel Crisis 2026: The Economic Turbulence Threatening African Skies and Global Trade
description:
A perfect storm of geopolitical shifts, refining bottlenecks, and logistics failures has birthed a global jet fuel (Jet A1) crisis that is doing far more than just delaying vacations.
It is reshaping the global travel landscape and, most urgently, threatening to derail the fragile economic progress of African nations.
When air travel becomes prohibitively expensive, the high-value supply chains—transporting electronics, fresh produce, and medical supplies—begin to snap.
Reshaping the Way We Move The 2026 crisis is forcing a fundamental rethink of global travel behavior.
The Bottom Line As we navigate the “empty skies” of 2026, it is clear that the jet fuel crisis is more than an industry problem; it is a global economic challenge.
text:
The year 2026 was supposed to be a hallmark for global connectivity, a time when the “new normal” of travel finally felt stable. Instead, the world’s aviation industry has hit a wall—or more accurately, a dry well. A perfect storm of geopolitical shifts, refining bottlenecks, and logistics failures has birthed a global jet fuel (Jet A1) crisis that is doing far more than just delaying vacations. It is reshaping the global travel landscape and, most urgently, threatening to derail the fragile economic progress of African nations.

From the bustling terminals of Heathrow to the strategic hubs in Lagos and Nairobi, the shortage is palpable. But while wealthier nations can often pivot or absorb costs, for many African economies, the inability to keep planes in the air is an existential threat.

The Global Ripple Effect

The crisis stems from a sharp decline in global refining capacity, coupled with disruptions in traditional oil supply routes through the Middle East. As Jet A1 stocks plummeted to decade lows earlier this year, the aviation industry saw an immediate, violent reaction.

Major international carriers have been forced to implement “fuel surcharges” that have sent ticket prices soaring by as much as 40% on long-haul routes. This isn’t just a headache for the luxury traveler; it is a direct blow to global commerce. When air travel becomes prohibitively expensive, the high-value supply chains—transporting electronics, fresh produce, and medical supplies—begin to snap.

Africa at the Epicenter

For Africa, the stakes are significantly higher. Aviation in Africa is not a luxury; it is a bridge. In a continent where road and rail infrastructure often lags behind, the “sky-highways” are what connect landlocked nations to global markets and regional neighbors to each other.

Nigeria as a Case Study:

The situation in Nigeria serves as a sobering warning for the rest of the continent. Despite being a major oil producer, the nation’s reliance on imported refined Jet A1 has left its domestic airlines vulnerable. Earlier this month, local ticket prices surged to unprecedented levels, making air travel a privilege reserved for the ultra-wealthy. When domestic flights stop, the internal gears of the continent’s largest economy begin to grind to a halt—affecting everything from the movement of agricultural goods to the flow of professional services.

Reshaping the Way We Move

The 2026 crisis is forcing a fundamental rethink of global travel behavior. We are seeing a “localization” of travel that hasn’t been witnessed in decades:

The Return of Regionalism: Travelers are increasingly opting for short-haul, regional trips that can be serviced by more fuel-efficient, smaller aircraft, abandoning long-haul “bucket list” journeys.

The Rise of Secondary Hubs: To save on fuel and airport fees, airlines are bypassing massive, expensive hubs in favor of smaller, more efficient regional airports.

The Digital Shift: As air travel costs become a significant line item on corporate balance sheets, we are seeing a resurgence in “virtual first” business culture, further dampening the demand for executive travel.

A Human Crisis in the Clouds

Beyond the macro-economic data lies a deeply human story. It’s the story of the small business owner in Rwanda who can no longer afford to fly to international trade fairs to find buyers for her textiles. It’s the story of families separated by thousands of miles who find their annual reunions priced out of reach.

Moreover, the high cost of fuel is slowing down the “humanitarian air bridge.” Relief organizations operating across the Sahel and Central Africa have reported that their operational costs have doubled, meaning less aid reaches those in desperate need because more of the budget is being swallowed by the fuel tank.

Is There a Way Out?

The 2026 crisis is a loud, uncomfortable wake-up call for the industry to move toward Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF)and more localized refining. African leaders are increasingly calling for “energy sovereignty”—the ability to refine aviation fuel on the continent rather than exporting crude only to buy back Jet A1 at a premium.

While the current turbulence is severe, it may eventually lead to a more resilient, localized, and green aviation sector. However, the transition period is proving to be a painful one.

The Bottom Line

As we navigate the “empty skies” of 2026, it is clear that the jet fuel crisis is more than an industry problem; it is a global economic challenge. For Africa, the goal is clear: build resilience or be left behind. The world is watching to see if the aviation industry can innovate its way out of this shortage before the economic damage becomes permanent.

text: Sustainable Aviation Fuel can no longer be treated as a regulatory compliance exercise. Aviation is entering an era where fuel strategy, energy security, emissions exposure, and operational resilience are becoming inseparable. The industry today has seven recognised SAF pathways under ASTM certification frameworks HEFA, ATJ, FT-SPK, FT-SKA, CHJ, SIP, and PtL/e-SAF each with different maturity, feedstock, scalability, and lifecycle carbon profiles. The critical question is no longer whether SAF works; it is which pathway aligns with a nation’s real feedstock base, industrial capability, and long-term aviation demand curve. For India, the answer is increasingly clear. While HEFA remains the fastest near term solution, its feedstock ceiling limits strategic scalability. Algae remains promising but operationally challenged due to contamination control, water intensity, biosecurity exposure, and open-culture bird attraction risks. The most scalable and operationally aligned pathway for India through the 2030–2045 window is cellulosic ATJ and future FT-SPK built around agricultural residue. India’s advantage is not imported feedstock it is biomass already available in its fields. The nations and airlines that move beyond “minimum compliance” and build indigenous SAF ecosystems early will ultimately control not only carbon exposure, but long term fuel resilience, energy sovereignty, and strategic competitiveness. title: Why Global Aviation Policy Must Reform for Future Travel Demand
description:
Global air travel is forecast to more than double by mid century, putting mounting pressure on governments to overhaul aviation policy so airports can expand capacity, meet climate goals and keep future travel affordable and reliable.
At the same time, the United Nations aviation agency has adopted a long term global aspirational goal of net zero carbon emissions from international aviation by 2050.
Studies from energy and aviation consultancies suggest that scaling sustainable aviation fuel production to levels consistent with net zero trajectories will demand very large capital commitments and long term offtake arrangements.
The adoption of long term climate goals and strategic plans at the global level reflects a growing recognition that uncoordinated national policies could undermine both sustainability and connectivity.
Analysts increasingly contend that the next phase of aviation policy reform will need to focus on closing this gap between global aspirations and national action.
text:
Global air travel is forecast to more than double by mid century, putting mounting pressure on governments to overhaul aviation policy so airports can expand capacity, meet climate goals and keep future travel affordable and reliable.

Traffic Forecasts Collide With Sustainability Pledges

Long term industry projections indicate that global passenger numbers will continue to rise steadily through 2050, with international bodies describing a return to the sector’s pre pandemic growth trajectory. Recent outlooks from airline and manufacturer studies point to compound annual growth rates in the range of about 3 to 4 percent over the next two decades, implying that worldwide traffic could more than double by mid century.

At the same time, the United Nations aviation agency has adopted a long term global aspirational goal of net zero carbon emissions from international aviation by 2050. A strategic plan released for the 2026 to 2050 period sets a vision in which air transport supports economic development while reducing its climate impact, including interim collective targets such as a 5 percent reduction in carbon dioxide emissions from cleaner energies by 2030.

This combination of rising demand and tightening climate commitments is reshaping debates over airport expansion. Publicly available information shows that governments are increasingly expected to ensure that new runways, terminals and airspace systems are compatible with national climate strategies, rather than simply adding capacity whenever congestion appears.

Industry studies from consulting and research groups indicate that reaching net zero while serving a much larger traveling public will require rapid gains in aircraft efficiency, large scale deployment of sustainable aviation fuel and new energy infrastructure on the ground. Without coordinated global policies, analysts warn that uneven regulation and fragmented investment could leave airport systems struggling to cope with both environmental obligations and peak demand.

Airports Face Capacity Crunch and Investment Gaps

While global forecasts suggest robust long term traffic growth, the physical capacity of many major hubs is already stretched. Research on multi airport systems in large metropolitan regions highlights how runways, gates and terminal space have become critical scarce resources, with environmental and land use constraints often limiting traditional expansion options.

Airports in fast growing regions of Asia, the Middle East and parts of Africa are planning significant development programs, but reports from airport associations and financial analysts point to substantial funding gaps. In Europe, for example, recent discussions around infrastructure needs have cited multi hundred billion euro investment requirements by 2040 to modernize facilities, integrate new energy systems and maintain competitive service levels.

Policy choices play a central role in whether this investment materializes. Some national frameworks still rely heavily on public funding for regional airports while restricting support for revenue generating projects, which can limit the ability of smaller facilities to scale sustainably. In other cases, passenger caps, noise limits or complex planning rules are affecting how quickly capacity can be added at primary hubs, even when demand is rising sharply.

Analysts argue that unless governments update these frameworks, more airports are likely to face chronic congestion, schedule constraints and higher operating costs. That in turn could translate into higher airfares, reduced connectivity for secondary cities and increased pressure on overburdened hubs. Modernized policy is seen as essential to unlocking private capital, encouraging efficient slot use and channeling investment toward projects that support both growth and emissions reduction.

Decarbonizing Airport Systems Requires Coherent Policy Signals

Beyond managing traffic, airports are being asked to transform into low carbon energy and mobility hubs. Initiatives coordinated by international forums and industry groups are promoting the concept of airports as platforms for sustainable aviation fuels, hydrogen and electrified ground operations, with the aim of aligning local infrastructure with the aviation sector’s 2050 climate targets.

To make that transformation viable, clear and stable policy signals are required. Studies from energy and aviation consultancies suggest that scaling sustainable aviation fuel production to levels consistent with net zero trajectories will demand very large capital commitments and long term offtake arrangements. Airports are expected to play a key role in storage, blending and distribution, but many lack regulatory frameworks that define responsibilities, cost recovery and standards for new fuel types.

Similarly, the deployment of hydrogen or high capacity electric charging for future aircraft will depend on close coordination between aviation regulators, energy ministries and local authorities. Publicly available assessments emphasize that grid upgrades, pipeline infrastructure and safety regulation need to evolve in parallel, or else individual airport projects risk becoming stranded investments.

Global policy initiatives, such as the framework on sustainable aviation fuels and other cleaner energies agreed under the UN aviation system, are intended to reduce this risk by setting common principles around planning, regulatory approaches, implementation support and financing. However, implementation still relies heavily on national action, meaning that inconsistent policies could slow the rollout of greener airport infrastructure even as traffic continues to climb.

Slot Rules and Market Access Under Scrutiny

As capacity tightens at popular hubs, regulators are also reexamining how scarce runway and gate slots are allocated among airlines. Research on congested multi airport regions describes how slot coordination rules and prioritization mechanisms influence which routes are served, how often and by which carriers.

Many of today’s slot systems were designed primarily to manage congestion rather than to optimize for climate goals or resilience. Recent academic work on capacity allocation under carbon constraints illustrates how integrating environmental considerations, such as carbon pricing or emissions performance, into slot decisions can shift airlines’ incentives toward more efficient aircraft and schedules.

Policy debates have also emerged around the balance between incumbent and new entrant carriers, as well as between full service and low cost operators. Industry commentary suggests that inflexible slot regimes can lock in historical patterns of service, limiting competition and making it harder to introduce newer, cleaner fleets at scale. Conversely, abrupt changes to access rules can unsettle investment plans and create uncertainty for airport revenues.

Several jurisdictions are now considering slot reforms that would more explicitly reward efficient use of capacity and support sustainability objectives, while maintaining predictability for long term planning. Observers note that aligning these reforms across regions will be important to avoid distortions in international networks and to preserve fair access to constrained global hubs.

Coordinated Global Governance Emerging but Uneven

International governance structures for aviation have been adapting to these pressures, but progress remains uneven. The adoption of long term climate goals and strategic plans at the global level reflects a growing recognition that uncoordinated national policies could undermine both sustainability and connectivity.

According to published coverage of recent assemblies and conferences, member states have increasingly endorsed collective benchmarks for emissions reduction and have supported frameworks intended to guide national policy on cleaner fuels, technology and infrastructure. These processes are designed to provide a common direction for regulators, airports, airlines and investors as they make decisions that will shape the industry for decades.

However, implementation timelines, regulatory detail and financial support vary widely between regions. Some governments are moving quickly to integrate aviation into broader climate legislation, carbon markets and energy transition plans, while others prioritize capacity growth and connectivity with less emphasis on emissions. This divergence creates uncertainty for airports planning multi decade investments, particularly in emerging markets where demand growth is strongest.

Analysts increasingly contend that the next phase of aviation policy reform will need to focus on closing this gap between global aspirations and national action. For airports, that means clearer long term guidance on climate requirements, market access rules and funding mechanisms. Without such reforms, the sector risks facing a mismatch between the infrastructure available on the ground and the travel demand expected in the skies.

text:
Bayer wants farmers to grow more camelina, an oilseed crop that resembles canola.

On May 6, Bayer and BP announced what they’re calling a “strategic alliance” to increase production of camelina in North America and around the globe. That camelina will be processed into biofuel such as renewable diesel and aviation fuel.

The strategic alliance should give farmers in southern Saskatchewan and other parts of North America more certainty that there’s a stable market for camelina in future years.

A win for customers and renewables

“We are utilizing our industry leading breeding program to enhance the crop and its untapped potential globally to help meet the needs of this growing market (for biofuels),” said Frank Terhorst, head of strategy and sustainability at Bayer Crop Science.

“We see this as a win for our customers and their farms, as it creates potential new revenue streams, but also a win for the renewable fuels market.”

The biofuel market math

Bayer and BP estimate that the market for biodiesel, renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) markets will triple by 2040, reaching 40 billion gallons. BP is a global energy company with annual revenues of nearly US$200 billion.

Camelina is an ideal feedstock for biofuel production because it can be grown in drier climates and lighter soils, such as the brown soil zone of the Prairies.

Bayer has already launched Newgold brand, a line of oilseed crops, which includes a spring and winter camelina.

Bayer is hoping that farmers in Montana, southern Saskatchewan and Alberta will plant camelina on marginal or under-utilized land, or between crops.

“Camelina is winter hardy, offering pod shatter resistance and drought tolerant characteristics allowing it to be grown on idle or fallow land … allowing farmers to avoid potential competition with food production,” Bayer says in a May 6 press release.

In 2025, Antoine Bernet, country division head with Bayer Crop Science in Canada, said Canadian farmers have a huge opportunity to supply the growing demand for biofuels.

To meet that demand, Bernet estimated the world may need an additional 120 million acres of oilseed crops.

To help producers, so they can grow the necessary feedstocks, Bayer began working on a portfolio of oilseed crops, now known as Newgold.

From Smart Earth to Newgold

That project accelerated in January 2025, when Bayer acquired the seed and IP assets of Smart Earth Camelina from Saskatoon.

For years, Smart Earth contracted camelina production in Western Canada and sold camelina oil into the horse, pet and fish food markets.

However, the company struggled to convince producers to grow camelina, with acreage rarely topping 10,000 acres on the Prairies.

With Bayer and BP now backing camelina, farmers might have more confidence in the crop.

Camelina is more tolerant of drought and dry growing conditions, so growers struggling with canola and poor canola yields in southwestern Saskatchewan may be willing to give it a try.

“This (geography) is exactly the opportunity,” Bernet said, while standing next to a camelina plot at the Bayer research centre near Saskatoon in 2025.

“These crops (camelina) can produce a high level of yield per acre, with a very low carbon intensity.”

text:
DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — A cargo ship caught fire Sunday after being hit by an unknown projectile off Qatar's coast, the British military said, in the latest attack on vessels in the Persian Gulf since a shaky ceasefire stopped fighting between the U.S. and Iran.

The Trump administration says the month-old ceasefire remains in effect. But it has been repeatedly tested with Iran restricting traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a strategic waterway key to the global flow of oil, and the U.S. imposing a blockade of Iranian ports.

Washington has been awaiting Iran's response to a new proposal for a deal to end the war, reopen the strait to shipping and roll back Iran's nuclear program.

One of the main sticking points in the negotiations is the fate of Iran's stockpile of highly enriched uranium. The U.N. nuclear agency says Iran has more than 440 kilograms (970 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60% purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels.

In an interview with Iranian state media, a spokesman for the Iranian military said that forces were on "full readiness" to protect nuclear sites where the uranium is stored.

"We considered it possible that they might intend to steal it through infiltration operations or heliborne operations," Brig. Gen. Akrami Nia told the IRNA news agency late Saturday. He didn't offer further details.

The majority of Iran's highly enriched uranium is likely still at its Isfahan nuclear complex, the head of the U.N. nuclear agency told The Associated Press last month.

The Isfahan facility was bombarded by U.S.-Israeli airstrikes in the 12-day war last year, and faced less intense attacks in this year's war.

In Sunday's naval attack, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre said that the strike caused a small fire on the ship, which was extinguished. The attack happened 23 nautical miles (43 kilometers) northeast of Qatar's capital, Doha, the UKMTO said.

There were no reported casualties, it said. It gave no details on the owner or origin of the ship, and there was no claim of responsibility.

But there have been several attacks against ships in the Persian Gulf over the past week. On Friday, the U.S. struck two Iranian oil tankers after it said that the vessels were trying to breach its blockade of Iran's ports.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard navy on Sunday reiterated its warning that any attack on Iranian oil tankers or commercial vessels would be met with a "heavy assault" on one of the U.S. bases in the region and enemy ships.

U.S. President Donald Trump has reiterated threats to resume full-scale bombing, if Iran doesn't accept an agreement to reopen the strait and roll back its nuclear program. Iran has mostly blocked the critical waterway for global energy since joint strikes on Feb. 28 by the U.S. and Israel launched the war, which has caused a global spike in fuel prices and rattling world markets.

America is racing to produce sustainable aviation fuel at a scale that could make commercial flying dramatically cleaner within the next ten years without changing a single aircraft engine.

Aviation is one of the hardest sectors to decarbonize — and one of the fastest growing. Global air travel is projected to double by 2040. Batteries are nowhere near capable of powering long-haul commercial aircraft. Hydrogen requires completely redesigned planes and fueling infrastructure. The most practical near-term solution is sustainable aviation fuel — drop-in replacement jet fuel that runs in existing engines while cutting lifecycle carbon emissions by up to 80%.

The United States produces more SAF than any other country — and has barely started. World Energy's Paramount facility in California is the largest dedicated SAF production facility in North America. Gevo, Fulcrum BioEnergy, and SkyNRG Americas are building additional capacity across the country.

United Airlines, Delta, American, and Southwest have all signed multi-year SAF supply agreements running into billions of gallons, providing the demand certainty that production investors need to commit capital at scale. The Biden administration set a SAF Grand Challenge target of 3 billion gallons annually by 2030 — enough to supply 10% of US aviation fuel demand with clean alternatives.

America burns more jet fuel than any other country. It is now determined to clean up what it burns.

text:
Trash for one person can become a valuable resource for another — and, increasingly, a profitable business model.

That was the message of the first session of H.eco Tech Festa 2026, where entrepreneurs and corporate leaders showed how waste materials ranging from used cooking oil to discarded firefighting suits and industrial wastewater are being turned into high-value resources and global business opportunities.

The session, titled “From Sustainable Ideas to the Global Market,” was held Thursday at Yonsei University's Baekyangnuri Hall as part of Herald Corp.’s eco-tech forum.

Moderated by Lee Han-kyung, CEO of Eco&Partners, the session saw four businesses that are already proving how environmental solutions can become profitable industries.

Lee Chung-ho, CEO of ReFeed, introduced a climate-tech business model that collects and digitizes waste cooking oil for use as sustainable aviation fuel.

“By 2050, airlines around the world must achieve net-zero emissions, and sustainable aviation fuel made from used cooking oil is becoming one of the most important solutions,” Lee said.

ReFeed currently operates in South Korea, Vietnam and India, managing waste cooking oil supply chains through digital collection and quality verification systems. The company has also obtained ISCC certification, an international sustainability certification widely used in global biofuel markets.

Lee said the global sustainable aviation fuel market is expected to grow to roughly $157 billion by 2030, adding that transparent data and supply-chain management will become critical competitive advantages.

“What I learned while building the company is that money often comes from doing what others avoid,” he said. “We carried dirty oil containers ourselves, and the data we gathered became our strongest asset.”

He also described how ReFeed expanded into Vietnam early on after identifying weak waste oil management systems there, later combining overseas operations with research and development support from the Korean government.

The company now aims to move beyond collection and enter fuel production itself, with ambitions of becoming what Lee described as “the next Aramco of the energy transition era.”

Lee Seung-woo, CEO of 119REO, introduced the company’s upcycling business that transforms used firefighting suits into high-performance industrial and safety materials.

“About 70 tons of firefighter protective suits are discarded every year, but the material is extremely difficult to recycle because it is made from aramid fibers that are five times stronger than steel,” Lee said.

He explained that the company was inspired by the story of late firefighter Kim Beom-seok, who battled cancer after exposure to hazardous substances during firefighting operations.

119REO developed technology to extract aramid fibers from used firefighting suits and reuse them in fire containment devices designed to prevent lithium battery fires on airplanes.

The company currently supplies the products to nine domestic airlines.

“Upcycling in the past appealed mainly to environmental values,” Lee said. “Now, recycled products must outperform conventional products in order to win the market.”

He added that the company is targeting the global aviation safety market, where fire containment devices could eventually be installed under every airplane seat.

Yang Hee-gyoung, CEO of KARI, presented technology that recovers high-purity resources from industrial wastewater generated during secondary battery manufacturing.

Industrial wastewater from battery production often contains toxic heavy metals and high concentrations of sulfuric compounds, making treatment technically difficult and expensive.

“Instead of simply evaporating wastewater and landfilling the remaining waste, we separate valuable materials at the molecular level through a combination of five integrated technologies,” Yang said.

The recovered materials can then be reused in products such as pharmaceutical ingredients and agricultural fertilizers, forming what Yang described as a new resource circulation value chain.

Yang also shared lessons from building the company as a startup, saying KARI constructed its own factory and accumulated operational data before securing large corporate clients in order to establish credibility in the market.

Kim Hye-sun, head of government affairs, public policy and sustainability compliance for Korea and Japan at HP, said sustainability has already become a major source of revenue for global companies.

“More than 60 percent of HP’s approximately 80 trillion won ($54 billion) in revenue in 2024 came from sustainable product lines,” Kim said. “Environment is no longer optional. It has become a business imperative.”

Kim said around 80 percent of environmental impact is determined during the product design stage, leading HP to focus on circular product design that improves repairability and recyclability from the beginning.

She also emphasized the importance of supply-chain management, noting that HP works with approximately 13,000 partners to manage carbon footprints across its value chain.

text:
Environmental challenges are no longer treated simply as matters of corporate responsibility, but as markets in their own right, creating new opportunities for companies, investors and young professionals, speakers said Thursday at H.ecoTech Festa 2026 in Seoul.

Hosted by Herald Media Group at Yonsei University’s Baekyang-Nuri Event Hall, the forum brought together entrepreneurs, corporate executives, sustainability experts and students to discuss how climate solutions and circular-economy industries are reshaping global markets.

Held under the theme “Circular Economy: Environment Is Money, Eco, Money, Me,” the event drew some 500 participants and featured discussions on climate-tech startups and future career opportunities in sustainability-related sectors.

In his opening remarks, Choi Jin-young, publisher and CEO of Herald Media Group, said responding to the climate crisis has become “a key engine for creating new economic value.”

“The environment is now one of the fastest-growing markets, one of the most powerful technologies and the starting point of new wealth creation,” Choi said.

Kim Yong-ho, executive vice president for administration and development at Yonsei University, said environmental value is increasingly becoming central to economic growth and career development.

“Our task is to help younger generations transform environmental values into real career assets,” Kim said.

The event opened with a performance by Raf Sandou, a Yonsei University alumnus known for appearing on the rap competition show “Show Me the Money 12.”

Holding a reusable cup on stage, Raf Sandou encouraged participants to think about how clothing is produced, consumed and discarded, saying sustainable consumption itself can become part of culture and style.

Science communicator Orbit later delivered a special lecture arguing that environmental businesses must become attractive and culturally appealing in order to drive meaningful behavioral change.

“People do not buy products simply because they are environmentally friendly,” Orbit said. “Successful eco-friendly businesses must become attractive products themselves.”

Citing Tesla as an example, Orbit said the electric vehicle-maker succeeded not by promoting sacrifice or environmental guilt, but by making sustainability feel technologically advanced and desirable.

The forum’s first session focused on circular-economy businesses transforming waste materials into commercially viable products and services.

Lee Chung-ho, CEO of ReFeed, introduced a business model that converts used cooking oil into supply-chain resources for sustainable aviation fuel, while Lee Seung-woo, CEO of 119REO, showcased technology that recycles discarded firefighter uniforms into fire containment devices used by domestic airlines.

Yang Hee-gyoung, CEO of KARI Corp., discussed resource-recovery technologies for industrial wastewater generated during secondary-battery manufacturing. Kim Hye-sun, head of government affairs, public policy and sustainability compliance for Korea and Japan at HP Inc., explained how sustainable product lines account for more than 60 percent of HP’s annual revenue.

Moderating the session, Lee Han-kyung, CEO of Eco&Partners, said the circular economy is creating industries in which “one person’s waste becomes another person’s valuable resource.”

The second session examined how sustainability expertise is becoming an increasingly important source of competitiveness across industries, from finance and manufacturing to law and consulting.

Cho Sun-young, ESG team lead at Kakao Bank, said environmental initiatives are increasingly tied to customer trust and brand loyalty in the financial sector.

Jeong Soo-jeong, head of LG Electronics' ESG Strategy Planning Team, discussed how sustainability has become an important factor in global business competitiveness and investment decisions.

Yoon Yong-hee, a partner at law firm Yulchon, discussed how environmental regulations and ESG-related legal risks are reshaping corporate strategy, while Kim Kyeong-yeon, head of global strategy at Eco&Partners, emphasized the importance of cross-sector cooperation in climate projects.

The event concluded with a career mentoring program in which professionals from major companies met with students and young participants in small-group sessions to discuss practical career paths and opportunities in the growing eco-tech sector.

Organizers said the forum would serve as a networking platform connecting future talent with innovators and industry leaders working at the intersection of climate technology, business and sustainability.

text:
Cathay Pacific’s fuel surcharges have climbed sharply in recent months, driven by the spike in oil prices arising from the conflict in the Middle East.

Compared to the start of the year, passengers are now paying close to three times the surcharges, on top of the regular airport taxes and fees. That significantly erodes the value of what would otherwise be sweet spots — what good is a 9,000 miles Economy redemption to Taipei if you have to pay S$213 on top of it?

Well, there’s finally some modest relief on the horizon. With jet fuel prices easing slightly, Cathay Pacific has announced a 13% reduction in its fuel surcharges, effective 16 May 2026. While this is still a long way from pre-conflict levels, any respite is welcome at this point!

Cathay Pacific eases fuel surcharges

Cathay Pacific will lower its fuel surcharges by roughly 13% for all commercial and award tickets booked from 16 May 2026 onwards.

Again, I want to emphasise that the booking date is what matters, not the actual travel date. Fuel surcharges are locked in at the time you book your ticket, so you won’t have to pay a top-up should jet fuel prices subsequently increase (and you also won’t get a refund if they subsequently decline, unless of course you cancel and rebook).

title: The Iran war has made jet fuel twice as expensive. Should we be flying with cooking oil instead?
description:
Since it began with US-Israeli airstrikes in late February, the Iran war has grounded tens of thousands of flights and pushed jet fuel to its highest price in years.
The most accessible feedstock – and the one most people imagine when they think of sustainable jet fuel – is used cooking oil.
The European Commission has launched a programme called AccelerateEU, which includes measures to optimise jet fuel distribution between EU member states.

text:
Since it began with US-Israeli airstrikes in late February, the Iran war has grounded tens of thousands of flights and pushed jet fuel to its highest price in years. Europe's jet fuel inventories have fallen 50 per cent, and Goldman Sachs warned this week that stocks could drop below the International Energy Agency's (IEA) critical 23-day shortage threshold in June – with the UK identified as most at risk.

Many airlines are facing a financial crunch as a result, with jet fuel averaging $181 a barrel globally, roughly double its pre-war level. Lufthansa has axed 20,000 flights through October. Spirit Airlines collapsed after a government bailout fell through. American Airlines faces $4bn more in fuel costs this year, and Delta is looking at a $2bn spike in the second quarter alone.

The crisis has brought renewed attention to the hunt for other fuel sources, and there is one in particular that the industry has been talking about for years but is yet to deploy at scale. Known as sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, it is typically made from used cooking oil, agricultural waste, and captured carbon. But how close are we to actually flying planes with it?

SAF currently makes up just 0.7 per cent of global kerosene consumption, according to the International Air Transport Association. Around two million tonnes were produced last year. The IEA’s net zero scenario requires at least 250 million tonnes of SAF annually by 2050, while some think-tanks say we should be targeting closer to 500 million tonnes by that date.

The most accessible feedstock – and the one most people imagine when they think of sustainable jet fuel – is used cooking oil. Almost all SAF currently in use is made from it. But the global supply of waste cooking oil is finite.

"While it's difficult to assess exactly how much could be available, the figures you can find in the literature is something around 20 million tonnes maximum," says Frédérique Rigal, co-author of a study published earlier this year on how aviation can decarbonise and move to sustainable fuels. Whichever projection you go by, that’s a small fraction of what is required by 2050.

The next generation of SAF – made from woody waste, agricultural residues and fermented alcohol – is more scalable but not yet commercially deployed at meaningful volumes.

Rigal admits there are some “hard limitations” on how quickly SAF production can be scaled up, partly because it requires large amounts of land, and partly because existing producers are mostly geared towards making fuel for cars not planes.

But she says the biggest problem of all is the fact that airlines themselves are not committing to buy SAF in advance. “Airlines are not moving quickly enough and are not giving enough offtake promises to these projects so that they can be realised,” she says.

Instead of looking to new alternatives, the short-term response from airlines to the shortage has come from conventional sources. US refiners have stepped up production, with exports of jet fuel to Europe surging more than 400 per cent to 94,000 barrels per day in April compared to February, according to Kpler data. The European Commission has launched a programme called AccelerateEU, which includes measures to optimise jet fuel distribution between EU member states.

But supply chain bottlenecks will persist for months even if a peace deal is reached, analysts warn. And the dominoes are falling across regions. South Korea, which supplies more than 80 per cent of the US West Coast's jet fuel imports, has lost crucial crude from the Middle East, threatening West Coast supply.

Another alternative fuel is called electro-SAF or e-SAF, which uses green electricity to combine captured carbon with hydrogen produced from water electrolysis, creating a synthetic kerosene. There is no hard upper limit on how much e-SAF can be produced, but Rigal says it is constrained by investment and industrial capacity, not feedstock. It remains expensive, and the technology is still maturing.

The EU and UK have set mandates requiring airlines to blend increasing proportions of SAF into their fuel, with e-SAF submandates starting at 1.2 per cent in 2030. But airlines have been calling for those targets to be pushed back, citing a lack of available supply.

The producers say that’s not the case. In a collective letter to the European Commission, e-SAF developers said they "firmly disagreed" with airlines' assessment, stating that "a significant number of eSAF projects are currently under development across Europe" and that "many of these projects are progressing towards final investment decision and are designed to deliver volumes within the ReFuelEU timeframe".

Mahesh Roy, programme director for SAF at the Green Finance Institute, said the current crisis has begun to shift the conversation around these fuels. SAF mandates in the UK and EU have been almost entirely couched in the language of the climate crisis and sustainability. The Strait of Hormuz blockade has reframed them as a question of energy security and sovereignty.

"The energy trilemma was what they used to talk about – energy security, energy sustainability, and energy affordability," Roy says. "Now you can see that security and price are really driving what people are thinking about." The crisis has not changed what SAF is, he said, but it has changed who is asking about it and why.

Airlines that had already secured SAF supply agreements before the crisis are now quietly benefiting, because SAF supply chains do not run through the Middle East.

"The imperative has always been there, and now we're just being reminded that finding better technologies to do things isn't just about global warming, even though that's a very good reason to do it in the first place," Roy says.

The financial pressure on airlines to move faster on SAF is growing, regardless of the current crisis. Global airline compliance costs under environmental policies – SAF blending mandates, EU and UK emissions trading systems, and the UN's Corsia carbon offsetting scheme – are set to nearly quadruple to $48 billion by 2035, up 256 per cent from 2026, according to BloombergNEF research published this week.

Roy says the doubling of jet fuel prices had already changed the terms of the debate. "All of jet fuel is going up by this amount due to this conflict," he said.

"Those fluctuations can't be guaranteed not to happen again anytime soon. That reframes it – is this just something in the realm of net zero, or is it also something that can help reduce the cost and energy security burden placed on economies that rely on fossil fuel imports?"

European carriers face the heaviest burden. Ryanair's unit operating costs are projected to rise 38 per cent from environmental policies alone by 2035, pushing the airline's margin per available seat-kilometre into negative territory. Airlines are likely to pass higher costs onto passengers, reduce capacity, or reroute long-haul flights from European hubs to avoid the highest compliance costs – a shift that could itself increase emissions by lengthening journey distances.

The investment required to close the supply gap is staggering. According to the ATAG Waypoint 2050 report, total cumulative capital expenditure for new renewable fuel plants over 2020-2050 ranges from $4.2 trillion to $8.1 trillion, depending on SAF yield assumptions. For context, total global oil and gas capital expenditure over the entire period from 2014 to 2021 was also $4.2 trillion.

Can any of this respond to the current crisis? No, experts say. However, the direction of the travel is clear.

"It's probably something more like four or five years" before the projects currently in development begin producing meaningful volumes, Roy says.

"If you think that the Russian invasion of Ukraine was four years ago, and then if there was another similar shock in about four years' time, those projects that are being planned now – if they can get off the ground and be properly supported – then yeah, that would shift," he says.

text:
EMILY FENG, HOST:

Travel depends on fossil fuels, but the war in Iran has disrupted the global fuel supply, and that has sent prices soaring, which is why European airlines like Lufthansa and KLM have announced they are cutting flights. And other airlines could follow. This got us wondering. Could another fuel source help take us to the skies? We've brought in someone with the science chops to help us dig through this, Short Wave co-host Emily Kwong. Hi, fellow Emily.

EMILY KWONG, BYLINE: Hello, fellow Emily.

FENG: I want to start with the basics...

KWONG: Yeah.

FENG: ...Which is what is alternative aviation fuel, or what some people call sustainable aviation fuel or even SAF for short?

KWONG: Yeah, so these are jet fuels made from nonpetroleum sources. The most common is cooking oil, but you can also make SAF out of agricultural crops, municipal waste. There's even synthetic possibilities. And these fuels are compatible with today's airplanes. So the idea is to basically supplement what fuels planes with something cleaner.

FENG: Like, do to planes what we've done to cars by making a hybrid electric vehicle, for example?

KWONG: Yeah, it's like a blend of energy sources. That's a great comparison. And I got to say, even I, science believer, was skeptical at the idea of a plane powered by leftover french fry oil.

FENG: Really?

KWONG: Yeah. So the first thing I wanted to know is, is this even safe?

JOSHUA HEYNE: Absolutely. And, Emily, I'm pretty confident you have flown on a plane with some of this stuff on there.

KWONG: This is Joshua Heyne, the director of the Bioproducts, Sciences and Engineering Lab at Washington State University.

HEYNE: If you flew out of LAX within the last few years, it's likely been on a plane you've been on. So roughly 0.6% of the global jet fuel consumption is this used cooking oil and other fats, oils, greases.

KWONG: But the economics, the supply side of this, is really tricky.

FENG: Right. Is there enough leftover cooking oil in the world to power the entire global aviation industry?

KWONG: Not at all, no. Cooking oil is not going to be a silver bullet to decarbonize aviation. Heyne says what's needed is a diverse portfolio of different technologies so SAF can be produced at scale and be affordable enough for airlines to even want to buy it. I heard something similar from Nafisa Lohawala, a fellow with the think tank Resources for the Future.

NAFISA LOHAWALA: Basically, de-risking this market is a big challenge for investors, for private investors, to feel comfortable, you know, spending their money here.

KWONG: And that's why a new venture in the Pacific Northwest is trying to break through. So earlier this year, Alaska Airlines and Washington state leaders announced the Cascadia Sustainable Aviation Accelerator. The goal of this project is to diversify that alternative jet fuel portfolio. Heyne is the technical lead for the project and a self-described fuel nerd.

HEYNE: We are working with companies that take postanaerobic-digested human sewage and turn that into jet fuel.

KWONG: It's a real twist on another man's trash, but for planes.

FENG: Using human sewage? Wow.

KWONG: That is something that a team (ph) might explore in the lab. Yes, yes, yes.

FENG: How much of all this is aspirational, Emily?

KWONG: Yeah. I mean, so much more science needs to be done. It's so early. And these projects, I mean, they can fail. A recent Reuters investigation found that of the 165 SAF projects announced by airlines over the last few years, only 10 reported producing commercial volumes of SAF. Also, another critique of these fuels that's important to say - the biobased ones - is that they have a potential impact on land use and food prices. But the biggest hurdle, of course, is whether all these different groups - government, industry, scientific institutions - can even come together to develop SAF at scale.

FENG: That's Emily Kwong, the co-host of Short Wave, NPR's science podcast. Thank you, Emily.

KWONG: Thanks so much.

(SOUNDBITE OF AIR'S "LA FEMME D'ARGENT") Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

text:
EMILY FENG, HOST:

Millions of students in universities in K-12 districts had their data compromised this week as a hack took down Canvas. That's a classroom management tool used all over the country. The attack raised more than a few questions about student data privacy and schools' reliance on private software to run classes. NPR's Sequoia Carrillo has been following the story and joins us now. Hi, Sequoia.

SEQUOIA CARRILLO, BYLINE: Hi, Emily.

FENG: So what happened this week with Canvas?

CARRILLO: So on Thursday, Canvas went offline. If you have a student or teacher in your life, you might know the name. But if not, it's an education software with more than 30 million users. Lots of K-12 districts use it along with half of all higher education institutions in North America. It helps educators manage assignments, post course materials and conduct exams. And the timing of the hack really couldn't be worse. My colleague Rachel Treisman spoke to Damon Linker, a lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania, who described it.

DAMON LINKER: Somewhere in the country when the outage happened, there probably were people actually taking final exams on the platform when it crashed.

CARRILLO: Instead, students and teachers saw a black screen saying a ransomware group called ShinyHunters had hacked the platform, not once but twice during the week, and then demanded money in exchange for students' data. And in Canvas' case, that doesn't just mean names, addresses and student ID numbers are at risk, but also possibly grades and coursework. And the program is a centralized hub of data for many schools.

FENG: Grades? Coursework? Why target students? Why are hackers interested in this data?

CARRILLO: So it might sound counterproductive when you first think about it, right? Kids don't have the means to pay a ransom for their data, typically.

FENG: Right.

CARRILLO: But they also don't typically monitor their own credit or have alerts set up to flag unwanted loan or credit card applications. So bad actors can get away with using a student's identity sometimes for years before anyone catches on. And this is just the latest in a recent string of attacks targeting young people. Definitely the largest in one spot so far. But dozens of school districts have reported hacks in the last few years.

FENG: OK, what does this hack mean for Canvas? And what does it mean for other edtech companies in general?

CARRILLO: So I was recently talking to T. Philip Nichols. He's an associate professor at Baylor University who's really been ringing alarm bells around public schools' increasing reliance on private companies for a while. We were actually talking about a different story last week when he said, just imagine if one day, Google or Canvas decided to turn their products off. A lot of schools would not be able to function, and that really shows just how fragile we've built these systems to be. I called him back in the wake of this hack.

T PHILIP NICHOLS: This incident should give us pause, not because it's an aberration, but because it isn't. We'd be much better off if schools were as vigilant about protecting student data when there isn't a ransom note attached.

FENG: Very prescient. So what are the next steps here?

CARRILLO: So Canvas is back online. Its parent company, Instructure, has been very quiet about the hack, only offering an update once its systems were back up on Friday. And for immediate concerns, like whether students will get their grades on time or if exams can take place, things seem to have gone back to normal. Canvas says it is still conducting an investigation to see the extent of this attack. I chatted with Matt Radolec, a cybersecurity expert who's worked in negotiations with ShinyHunters before. And he said, even if the system is back online, that doesn't necessarily mean the data breach is over. He says once a group like that is in, it's very hard to make sure they're out. But for now, at least for final exam season, things seem to be running again.

FENG: That's Sequoia Carrillo with the latest on the Canvas hack. Thank you, Sequoia.

CARRILLO: Thank you. Transcript provided by NPR, Copyright NPR.

description:
ELISSA NADWORNY, HOST: Twenty years ago, Guy Goma went for a job interview at the BBC in London for a position in the IT department.
